title: Chapter 2.  History — From Ancient Settlement to British Rule

blocks.content: Lakshadweep's history chapter is comparatively compact relative to India's mainland UTs, but features a distinctive local sequence of religious conversion, Kerala-mainland political overlordship, and a notably late/limited period of direct British administration.

The islands' early settlement history is not precisely documented, but local tradition and limited historical evidence suggest settlement by seafaring peoples from the Kerala coast in ancient times, with the islands' Malayalam-related language and cultural ties to Kerala reflecting this mainland connection (Chapter 6).

Local Lakshadweep tradition attributes the introduction of Islam to the islands to the legendary figure Ubaidullah (sometimes associated with a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, though this account is traditional rather than rigorously documented), with conversion to Islam becoming near-total across the archipelago over subsequent centuries, making Lakshadweep India's only Union Territory/state with an almost entirely Muslim population (Chapter 6).
Kerala Mainland Overlordship: Cannanore & Arakkal Rule

For an extended period preceding formal British/colonial administration, various island groups of Lakshadweep came under the political and commercial overlordship of mainland Kerala rulers, most notably the Kolathiri Rajas of Cannanore (Kannur) and, later and most significantly, the Ali Rajas of Cannanore's Arakkal family — the only Muslim royal dynasty of Kerala, historically based in Cannanore, which held substantial commercial and administrative authority over several Lakshadweep islands.

This Arakkal-Cannanore connection is historically significant as one of the few instances in Indian history of an entirely Muslim ruling dynasty exercising authority in the Kerala region, and it shaped Lakshadweep's early administrative and commercial links to the Malabar coast well before formal British involvement.

★ EXAM POINT: The Arakkal family of Cannanore — Kerala's only Muslim royal dynasty — historically held authority over parts of Lakshadweep, a distinctive and specifically tested link between the islands and mainland Kerala's own unusual dynastic history.

The British gradually assumed administrative control over different island groups through the 18th and 19th centuries, generally acquiring authority (initially over revenue collection rights, later fuller administrative control) from the Arakkal family and other regional powers, integrating the islands into British India's Madras Presidency administrative structure by the 19th century.

Under British rule, the islands were administered with a relatively light and limited degree of direct intervention compared to much of the rest of British India, given their remoteness, small population, and limited perceived strategic/commercial significance at the time — a historical pattern of administrative distance that some scholars connect to the islands' subsequently distinct and protective post-Independence governance framework (Chapter 4).

items: Local tradition attributes Islam's introduction to the legendary figure Ubaidullah; conversion became near-total over subsequent centuries.
Arakkal family of Cannanore (Kerala's only Muslim royal dynasty) historically held authority over parts of Lakshadweep, alongside the Kolathiri Rajas.
Under British rule, the islands were part of the Madras Presidency, administered with comparatively light direct intervention.
